content:
(This is an idea I'm really stealing from @Sven Krippendorf ). Should we write a status report for Physlib, giving a summary of development so far, what has been contributed to etc, maybe with some stats? The idea would then be to 1) put it on the arXiv, and 2) submit it to a journal. People who have contributed (non-trivially) to Physlib would be welcome to be authors (listed alphabetically). This could be a good way in which we can give back some credit to those who do more of the service-work on projects like this. This would naturally not exclude others from writing papers on the more specifics of projects they have worked on. I believe such things are common in other areas of academia.

What are people's thoughts?

There is no harm in doing this at all. Physicists are generally more accustomed to reading papers than directly browsing GitHub repositories, so this could be a good way to attract more people. I thought it had been done previously. What we need to consider is what to write in this paper; perhaps we can refer to https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.09336.

I think the akin to https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.09336 is the paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08863. But I see these as a more of "Hey this project exists" type of thing.

I think what I am thinking here is something along the lines of: "You know that project we mentioned way back then, well over the las couple of years we have done a lot to it. Here is what, here is how it has grown, here is what we have learned, and here is how we see things going in the future." Though more of an executive summary rather than going into the nitty-gritty details.

I see what you mean. An updated report is a good idea, particularly to highlight the recent addition of quantuminfo. We could also use it to clearly outline our AI policy and list out future objectives and milestones, which would be very useful for guiding development.
Coming back to this: Maybe we should start an overleaf or a github for this report.

This would be good, however I don't have much experience in writing collaborative papers so I don't know which route to go, but if we do make a choice I don't mind setting it up. (If someone else isn't already taking the lead)

Is the PR process in github conducive to writing papers?

I started a (currently empty) GitHub here just a bit ago: https://github.com/jstoobysmith/PhyslibStatusReport

GitHub is probably not the best for this sort of thing, but given everyone who contributes to Physlib has an understanding of GitHub, it is probably easiest for now.
Maybe good to try and find similar papers we can base this on.

I was thinking as we look for papers to base on

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

"You know that project we mentioned way back then, well over the las couple of years we have done a lot to it. Here is what, here is how it has grown, here is what we have learned, and here is how we see things going in the future."

Maybe we could have a short discussion on this thread about what we think about these questions?
I'm yet to form an opinion on the above so it would be good to get a bit of a feel of what more experienced members of the community think about this.

(I just realized that the Joseph's message was not framed as questions, what i mean is how the project has grown? What has the community learned? and where do we see the project going? and who is the project for? )

I think some of these questions probably need fleshing out a bit; I personally find "What has the community learned?" quite difficult, because there are so many different aspects to the project his could related to e.g. the Lean code itself, the organisation of the project etc.

One way that I've come to think things is in terms of a 'project levels':

  • Community level -> Repository level -> Directory level -> Content level -> Infrastructure level

(never really sure where Infrastructure should go, or what is the right framing of any of this - maybe there is something already in software engineering along these lines.)

Maybe for each of these levels the right questions to be asking are:

  1. What does that level currently look like? (Summary)
  2. What has contributed to that?
  3. What works at this level?
  4. What doesn't work?
  5. Ideas for future improvements?

Maybe in a bit more detail.

Community level.

I think this covers things like: the Lean Zulip; the sorts of conversations that are happening on it for Physlib;
the sorts of people that are engaging actively within the channel; the cafes; the number of forks of the project; the number of pull requests etc.

Repository level

I think this covers the review process, the lean versions, and bumps of the lean versions etc, AI policy etc.

Directory level

The organisation of the directories, and files within them, the amount of coverage in different areas etc.

Content level

What is actually in the Lean file itself, any refactoring which are important, any new results we want to highlight, what is the cutting edge.

Infrastructure level

The website, any other search engines around the project, the AI tools, other infrastructure within the Lean code etc.

Mhm okay this makes alot of sense, and after a very brief reading on software engineering practices these levels seem to allign with their own model. Specifically on infrastructure, in SWE it seems to be related to automated building, linters, automatic documentation and website generation; so stuff that we have in physlib in some shape or form.

Regarding the workflow an idea floating in my head is that we can structure the paper's repository with folders matching the project levels (e.g., community/, infrastructure/). Contributors can draft their sections as .md files and submit them as PRs (with similar guidelines to physlib)?

My hope is that this would make the review process easier and also get an idea for what the content could be and get people's ideas. From there when the content is stable and organized, then a switch to .tex/overleaf?

What do people think regarding this?

I think this is a great idea. Generally I'm a big fan of .md files :). The only other thing we probably want to include are graphs etc. Would be nice to include those within the repo itself, so in a future date if we ever reproduce this we can follow that.

Should think how exactly we do the author list too.

I agree with graphs, it should be within the repo, so I think jupyter notebooks might be a good solution for prototyping?

With regards to authors, I liked the way mathlib's paper does it, the primary author was the "mathlib community" and they provided the authors/contributors to mathlib in the acknowledgements.
Yeah, I think this is how the CERN experiments do it also. Jupyter notebooks sound good!

I have a suggestion for the status report.

When I talk about Physlib with people working in high-energy physics, one of the most common questions I hear is: “How is Lean different from Mathematica?” This is a very reasonable question. Mathematica is already widely used in the high-energy physics community, and, from the outside, Lean and Mathematica may both appear to be tools for symbolic calculation.

My usual answer is that Lean allows us to build a formally verified mathematical structure in which statements and proofs can be checked automatically, whereas Mathematica is primarily a computational tool and does not provide the same kind of proof-level verification. However, I do not think we yet have a sufficiently clear and compelling example that demonstrates this distinction to physicists.

Joseph’s previous paper, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.08139, may provide one possible example. Still, I would especially like to find a case that can genuinely be described as “something that can only be done in Lean but not in Mathematica”. And it better to be some kind of large milestone theorem.

I think it would be valuable to identify such an example and mention it in the status report. It could help communicate the distinctive purpose and value of Physlib to the broader physics community.

I think this is a very valid point @Jinzheng Li , we should actively be looking to find such examples/theorems/topics within physlib, however I do think that we could think about this subject in 2 manners:

Event driven and I guess time/maturity driven, the point you have above might fall into the event driven category, when a formalization has been fully reviewed and accepted to merge into physlib, writing a detailed paper like @Joseph Tooby-Smith's 2HDM paper, Wicks theorem (I also believe other maintainers had written a paper regarding the quantum Stein's lemma?) is a great choice to make.

I think its good as you said, we should work towards not only identifying within physlib, but also actively selecting representative theorems/topics to include in physlib, building good API to properly envelope these topics and writing papers to elucidate what we learned and how this can help physics, which was I believe was mentioned in Joseph's first message on this thread (regarding writing papers on specific projects)

However, with regards to the status report, say if we do not have such an example within physlib at the moment, which can be polished and written into a paper for academic communication, would it be worth holding off on the status report?. Conversely, if such an example did exist at the moment, is the status report the right place to report the details of this information?

I myself am not sure about the above questions but would like to hear your thoughts

I've thought about Mathematica vs Lean quite a lot in the past, and have always found it hard to find a definite example of something along the lines of:

"Even without caring about verification, in Lean you could do this, but in Mathematica you can't."

After all both are Turing-complete programming languages, so all bets are off in trying to find a difference (for Lean you have to allow meta-programs for Turing completeness).

Given this, I think a better question is the following:

"When is Lean the better tool compared to Mathematica".

I think we likely have many examples of this in Physlib.

Would you have some examples in mind?, I do not have much experience with mathematica so it would be a great learning experience for me to read through the lean files and work out why lean is the better tool for this.

I agree with both of you.

And yes, the better question is, "When is Lean the better tool compared to Mathematica?" But I am looking for an example where Lean is clearly much better and where nobody would ever want to do it in Mathematica. I am not familiar with every area of PhysLibs, so there may already be some good examples. If someone asked you this question, which existing example would you bring up? @Joseph Tooby-Smith

Let me give two different points here (beyond the natural one, which is that Lean gives you verifiability)

Point 1 (Proofs): Lean is specifically designed for proofs. So, if I wanted to proof something slightly abstract, for example that the eigenvalues of the quantum harmonic oscillator form a basis of the Hilbert space, I would much rather do that in Lean then in Mathematica. I wouldn't even know where to start with this in Mathematica.

Point 2 (Encoding reasoning): I think an example can be drawn by looking at a complicated calculation in Physics. Let us take as an example, the calculation involved in finding the eigenvectors of a finite dimensional quantum mechanical system.

Suppose I didn't know what the eigenvectors were. I would almost certainly turn to Mathematica to find them. It is a computer algebra system, and designed for these sorts of computations.

However, if I wanted to understand the assumptions that went into that calculation, how it relates to other results, as well as have a version of it which is reusable so I can generalise it or push it forward, then I would use Lean.

Mathematica is very good at giving you new answers (to certain questions), Lean is very good at giving you, and storing, insight and structure within an answer, and allowing that answer to be reused.

Mhmm that makes alot of sense, it seems that the precise notion of logic/encoding reasoning seems to be the real advantage. However, the subtle point that you mentioned regarding understanding the assumptions is the biggest effect of having the ability to encoding reasoning (along side being able to store them).

I definitely see the utility of including such examples in the status report, maybe a section can be dedicated to just this point, where we tackle different areas of physics in physlib and how using lean 4 to formalize allowed us to see "deeper" into the assumptions/theory
.

I was planning on cloning the repo for the status report and opening a PR with some inital file structure and readme's (based on discussions in this thread), just to get things started.

This was the file structure I was thinking:

Community Engagement
Repo Management
Directory Scope
Content
Infrastructure
Examples from physlib

Are the names alright? I'm very open to suggestions
These look good to me!

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Maybe good to try and find similar papers we can base this on.

Regarding literature search, there's a free site https://www.undermind.ai/ that I've found very useful for crafting and executing searches of literature.

As an example, I started with the prompt

I'm in the early stages of writing a paper about use of Lean theorem prover to write proofs for mathematical physics. I have a large code base and there are multiple contributors. The paper I'm writing is intended to be an overview and status of the project. I need a literature search

Undermind.ai responded with

Your search should likely cover both formalization of mathematical-physics mathematics in Lean and the broader methods that make large, multi-contributor formalization projects maintainable—not just papers about Lean itself.

  1. Which mathematical-physics areas does the codebase focus on (for example, quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, relativity, field theory, or mathematical foundations)?

  2. Should the search prioritize closely related formalization projects and technical methods, or also include literature useful for the paper’s project overview—such as collaboration practices, library architecture, dependency management, and assessing project status?

To which I replied

Regarding the first question, the scope of the project is all of mathematical physics.

Regarding the second question, closely related formalization projects in physics would be more relevant

Undermind.ai then drafted the search as

I am writing an overview and status paper about a large, multi-contributor project that uses the Lean theorem prover to formalize mathematical physics. Search for closely related scholarly literature on formalizing mathematical physics in Lean, with emphasis on substantial projects, formal libraries, and applications across mathematical-physics areas. Include relevant formalization projects in physics using other interactive theorem provers when they provide useful direct comparison or context, but prioritize work most closely related to Lean-based mathematical-physics formalization. The results should help situate the project, explain its relationship to prior efforts, and assess the current state of the field.

Undermind then generated a bibtex file with these citations:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1YesU7rFoyyomm1DZjVkRiNP1PabzgwjEqcrXhute838/edit?usp=sharing

We should definitely still do the status report, but one thing we could do for the time being, or maybe in addition to this, is automatically generate a monthly report based on commits and diffs to Physlib. We could then automatically create a citation for that based on the people that have contributed to Physlib in that month. This may give something easy which people can cite, or similar.
Where do you envision this monthly report living?
I think just on the website - not planning on submitting them anywhere.

I'm currently working on implementing this feature with a table on the website where you can view a history of these generated reports and see PDFs for each one. I've only gone back to January so far as generating the report is quite slow
